title: A Metalinguistic Axiomatic Theory of Intelligent Systems: Formal Structures of Cognition, Knowledge, and Theoretical Systems
abstract: English abstractThis work develops a metalinguistic axiomatic framework for cognition, knowledge, theories, intelligent systems, and AI. At the cognitive level, the framework distinguishes objectified items, registered meta-level interfaces, and residual metalanguage, retaining failure and unevaluability. Evaluation, object admission, name binding, and state writeback each have separate conditions. At the knowledge level, knowledge-base membership is distinct from verified or assertable status. Provenance, composite status, four-valued judgment, argumentation, tracing, and safe introduction serve distinct roles. At the theory level, theory objects comprise object and relation sets under co-rootedness and well-founded dependency conditions. Theory evaluation, transformation, and positioning have separate conditional interfaces. At the intelligent-system level, maintenance constrains optimization. Boundary, stable, and higher-order intelligence depend on stated criteria; AI generation and model scale alone do not establish these qualifications. Behavioral interfaces conditionally connect complete action, interaction goals and evaluations, and traceable joint descriptions. A six-step metatheoretical workflow organizes the deconstruction, reconnection, and reconstruction of existing theories. Task-relative textual and geometric representations organize theoretical expression and retrieval without replacing the underlying theory texts. The contribution combines theory-internal axiomatic or quasi-axiomatic reconstruction with cross-level interface organization. It makes domains, dependencies, admissibility, failures, and theoretical effects explicit. Empirical scales, engineering realizations, and system effectiveness require independent implementation and testing.中文摘要认知、知识、理论、智能系统与人工智能研究常使用相互分离的概念语言。产生结果与引入对象、保存信息与接受知识、改善输出与维持系统等不同任务,也因此容易混淆。本文建立一套元语言公理化框架,通过对象层与元层接口连接这些研究层次。框架区分已对象化项目、已登记元语言接口,以及当前对象语言不能吸收的元语言余项,并保留失败与不可评价。 在认知与知识方面,框架分别规定求值、对象引入、名称绑定与状态写回的资格。知识库成员不等于已验证或可断言知识。来源、复合知识标签、主显示、四值判断、论证、回溯和安全引入各有职责;它们不构成所有候选必经的流水线。 在理论层,理论由对象集及其中的关系对象集构成,对象集须满足共根与依赖良基条件。原始对象与基本原理由内部前驱读取,理论品质、变换和结构位置则通过各自的条件接口处理。 在系统层,维持约束优化,边界、稳定和高阶智能按明示判据区分。AI的生成与规模本身不证明这些资格成立。行为附录通过条件接口接入完整行为结构、互动目标与评估,以及可追溯的联合描述。行为分类不等同于趋人化或主体资格。 前四章的部分接口被组织为六步流程,并由四组异质方法示例说明。收束命题仅在各步资格与输入输出条件成立时连接环节;示例本身不独立证明这些条件。第8章规定任务相关的文本与几何表示,并区分假设与待定承接位。索引调用受答案覆盖、局部正确性和完整成本约束。 本文结合选定概念的理论内重建与跨层接口组织,明确各项内容的对象域或元层角色、资格、依赖、失败值与理论效力。工程实现、经验量尺和系统效果仍需独立实现与检验。 Full texts and supplementary materialThis record provides the full text in English and Chinese, together with separate English and bilingual Chinese-English theory-framework diagrams to support reading and cross-referencing of the main text. Companion website: yipenggu.com (planned to go online before manuscript submission). 全文与补充材料本记录提供本理论的中英文全文,以及英文版和中英版理论框架图补充材料,供读者辅助理解、定位和对照正文。配套网站域名为yipenggu.com,计划于提交论文前上线。

title: Fooling Deep Neural Networks: A Strategyfor Mitigating DLSCA
abstract: Side-channel analysis (SCA), particularly deep learning-based SCA (DLSCA), threatens cryptographic implementations by automatically exploiting complex and nonlinear leakage and weakening countermeasures such as masking. Existing countermeasures against DLSCA mainly suppress, decorrelate, or obscure exploitable leakage. This work introduces Spoofing-based Mitigation (SPM), a leakage-shaping approach designed to mislead key-recovery attacks by biasing their key hypotheses. SPM introduces a controllable offset into AES intermediate-value computations and compensates for it to preserve the correct ciphertext, while shaping the relationship between measured leakage and the intermediate-value labels used for profiling. We implement SPM at the first-round S-box output and evaluate it at first-round and last-round attack points on an XMEGA128D4 microcontroller using a ChipWhisperer platform. Under the evaluated identity-label settings, the induced key’s rank rapidly reaches zero across seven CNN-based DLSCA models, two MLP-based models, and a template attack, while the correct key remains unrecovered. These results provide experimental evidence that leakage shaping can misdirect the evaluated key-recovery attacks. The collected dataset is publicly available to support reproducible research.

title: A Semantic Representation Model for Geographic Features with Integrated Neighborhood Context
abstract: Geospatial data contains abundant temporal, spatial, and attribute information related to geographic entities, serving as a critical foundation for the development of new quality productive forces. Achieving effective semantic representation of geographic features is a key prerequisite for enabling intelligent data analysis and application. Spatial relationships are an essential semantic characteristic of geographic features and are among the most commonly introduced characteristics for representation learning in recent studies. However, current research primarily focuses on point-based features (such as POIs) or on converting line and polygon features into point features, leading to inaccuracies in representing spatial proximity between features, which in turn affects the representation outcomes. In this paper, a feature unit delineation method based on geometric shapes is proposed to better construct the proximity relationship graph between features. It enriches the semantic features of feature units using a large language model and trains an edge optimization model to refine the graph structure. Building upon iGCL, a semantic representation learning model for geographic features is constructed. Finally, using Xiamen Island and Nanchang City as study areas, experimental datasets are built by integrating OSM and Amap (Gaode) POI data. The performance of the proposed model is validated and compared with other models through three tasks: semantic overlap calculation, node classification, and node clustering. The results show that the feature representations obtained by the proposed model achieve the best performance across all tasks, fully demonstrating its effectiveness and superiority in geographic feature representation learning, thereby providing a foundation for subsequent intelligent geographic feature tasks.

evidence.title: A Semantic Representation Model for Geographic Features with Integrated Neighborhood Context
evidence.abstract: Geospatial data contains abundant temporal, spatial, and attribute information related to geographic entities, serving as a critical foundation for the development of new quality productive forces. Achieving effective semantic representation of geographic features is a key prerequisite for enabling intelligent data analysis and application. Spatial relationships are an essential semantic characteristic of geographic features and are among the most commonly introduced characteristics for representation learning in recent studies. However, current research primarily focuses on point-based features (such as POIs) or on converting line and polygon features into point features, leading to inaccuracies in representing spatial proximity between features, which in turn affects the representation outcomes. In this paper, a feature unit delineation method based on geometric shapes is proposed to better construct the proximity relationship graph between features. It enriches the semantic features of feature units using a large language model and trains an edge optimization model to refine the graph structure. Building upon iGCL, a semantic representation learning model for geographic features is constructed. Finally, using Xiamen Island and Nanchang City as study areas, experimental datasets are built by integrating OSM and Amap (Gaode) POI data. The performance of the proposed model is validated and compared with other models through three tasks: semantic overlap calculation, node classification, and node clustering. The results show that the feature representations obtained by the proposed model achieve the best performance across all tasks, fully demonstrating its effectiveness and superiority in geographic feature representation learning, thereby providing a foundation for subsequent intelligent geographic feature tasks.

title: Algorithmic Opacity, Proxy Discrimination and Financial Citizenship in AI-Driven Credit Markets
abstract: Abstract: This article investigates the intersection of artificial intelligence, consumer credit, and financial governance, arguing that algorithmic opacity in AI-driven credit scoring does not eliminate discrimination but transforms it into an epistemic and governance crisis. Drawing on doctrinal legal analysis, comparative regulatory examination of Brazil, the European Union, and the United States, and an analytical reconstruction of the Apple Card case, the study demonstrates that historical biases are statistically reconstructed through proxy variables while the inherent opacity of machine learning models conceals these processes under a veneer of data-driven objectivity. The result is a structural deficit in evidence, contestability, and supervisory capacity that undermines the core pillars of financial citizenship: protection, participation, and trust. The original contribution lies in reconceptualizing algorithmic credit discrimination as a problem produced by opacity rather than solely by intentional disparate treatment, revealing that the absence of evidence of bias cannot be equated with evidence of fairness when the system under scrutiny is designed in ways that resist independent verification.

title: Research on fine-tuning and application of domain-specific large language model for traditional Chinese medicine consultation
abstract: To address the issues of insufficient professional knowledge and low accuracy in question answering within the field of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) using general-purpose language models, this paper proposes a method for constructing a TCM question-answering model by fine-tuning a pre-trained language model. First, relevant TCM literature and diagnostic knowledge are collected and organized to construct a domain-specific question-answering dataset, achieving a structured expression of TCM knowledge. Second, instructions are fine-tuned on the pre-trained language model to adapt it to question-answering tasks within the TCM domain. Finally, experimental validation is conducted in TCM consultation and knowledge-based question-answering scenarios, and the model is compared with the non-fine-tuned model. Experimental results show that the proposed method can effectively improve the accuracy and professionalism of the model's question-answering in the TCM field, demonstrating its potential value for intelligent TCM consultation applications.

title: Bipartite Concept-to-Token Language Modeling: Paraphrase-Invariant Mini Concept Planners with Context-Steered Token Expansion
abstract: Autoregressive token-level Large Language Models (LLMs) conflate high-level semantic planning with low-level syntactic realization, expending O(L2) self-attention compute across surface tokens even when underlying clauses represent deterministic, paraphrase-invariant concepts. Conversely, pure sentence-level Large Concept Models (LCMs) compress en- tire clauses into continuous embeddings but lose exact syntactic and lexical steering at branching transitions. We propose the Bipartite Concept-to-Token Architecture (BCTA), which decouples language modeling into two specialized networks: (1) a Stage-1 Mini Concept Planner that operates on canonical, paraphrase-invariant concept codes (map- ping synonymous spans such as “sun rises in the east” and “sun rises in eastern direction” to a single quantized representation SRIE) interleaved with structural steering operators (<$>) to predict the next semantic state (SSIW) in O((L/k)2) complexity; and (2) a Stage- 2 Context-Steered Token Expansion Model that frames the planned sequence [SRIE, <$>, SSIW]into fluent subword tokens conditioned on global entity premises (e.g., <we have one sun> → “The sun rises in the east and that same sun sets in the west”) and a lightweight residual detail bypass that preserves exact numerical and lexical literals. We formulate the complete composite objective combining Paraphrase-Invariant Vector Quan- tization, Anti-Collapse InfoNCE, and Context-Contrastive Margin losses, differentiate BCTA from concurrent multiscale concept architectures, and detail the exact implementation blueprint for both a 15.2M-parameter Mini Prototype and a 3.8B-parameter Expanded Model.

title: Brandora: Automating Brand-Compliant Marketing Content Creation with Retrieval- Grounded Cloud Generative AI
abstract: General-purpose generative models used for advertising often invent prices, discounts, certifications and environmental claims that a brand cannot support. This paper presents Brandora, a hybrid edge and cloud generative AI system that drafts advertisement copy and visuals grounded in a company's own product catalogue and brand guidelines. A retrieval-augmented generation pipeline retrieves the catalogue records closest to a marketer's brief and always adds every mandatory guideline to the context of a locally hosted large language model, which returns a structured brief listing its sources and the requested details it could not support. A text-free prompt is sent to a serverless text-to-image model on Cloudflare Workers AI, and the approved copy is typeset onto the returned image, which avoids the malformed lettering that diffusion models produce. A reviewer approves every poster and each decision is written to an audit log. The paper also specifies extensions to the same architecture and an evaluation protocol of sixty briefs, including adversarial requests, for measuring guideline violations, grounding precision, image text artifacts, latency and reviewer effort. On 200 development queries, the hybrid retrieval stage ranks the correct product first in 97.5 percent of cases.

title: Use First, Verify Later: AI Mathematical Discovery and the Operative Standards of Acceptance
abstract: When AI mathematical discovery outpaces human verification, social demand can force time-bound decisions about adoption. The HYC theorem distinguishes two directions: HYC1 identifies operative standards when duty-bound institutions cannot verify or abstain; HYC2 reconstructs such standards from decisions already issued without verification. Historical cases show that use, formal checking, and understanding can occur at different times. AI may also build on unverified results before human checks finish. Where society has no urgent demand, researchers can defer adoption, provided they retain time and an independently auditable record. Information saturation may undermine that capacity.

title: Il diritto di dubitare Privacy, pensiero critico e approccio Human-Tech nell'era dell'intelligenza artificiale
abstract: Nel confronto con l’intelligenza artificiale generativa, l’abilità decisiva potrebbe non essere formulare richieste semprepiù sofisticate, quanto preservare la libertà di mettere in discussione risposte convincenti. Il contributo propone unapproccio Human-Tech centrato su agency, verifica, protezione dei dati e responsabilità della decisione. Integrandopsicologia del ragionamento, studi sull’affidamento eccessivo all’AI e indicazioni istituzionali su privacy e alfabetizzazionedigitale, viene delineato un modello operativo in cinque movimenti: definire, proteggere, esplorare, falsificare eassumersi la decisione. Si esaminano esempi per scuola, formazione e contesti organizzativi, con attenzione alle nuovegenerazioni e alle implicazioni sociali della delega tecnologica. L’obiettivo non è contrapporre umano e artificiale, bensìprogettare relazioni con la tecnologia capaci di aumentare possibilità senza indebolire il giudizio.

title: Adaptive Confidence-Aware Transformer–Graph Fusion Network for Robust Credit Fraud Detection
abstract: Currently, finding fraudulent transactions made with credit card systems is a major concern for the research community. The growth of online payment systems has increased transaction volumes. Attackers use increasingly sophisticated techniques, including identity theft, card cloning, and the compromise of online transactions, making fraud detection challenging for financial institutions. Traditional detection models rely on fixed rules and thresholds, which limit their ability to adapt to emerging fraud patterns; these systems are not flexible to deal with new and dynamic types of fraud. The literature shows growing interest in the development of datadriven intelligent systems for the analysis of transactional behaviors and the automatic recognition of suspicious activities. In this context, an adaptive confidence-aware transformer–graph fusion network model is proposed for reliable fraud detection in imbalanced financial transaction datasets. This study empirically investigates the two publicly available financial transaction datasets: ULB credit card and PaySim synthetic dataset which is a commonly used standard in the literature, examining fraud detection; these datasets have realistic distributional characteristics and anonymized variables. The graph-based fusion model is evaluated on PaySim, where it obtains 99% in accuracy, 96 % in F1-score, and 99 % in receiver operating characteristic-area under the curve (ROC-AUC). It improves recall and F1-score compared to individual transformer and Graph Sample and Aggregate (GraphSAGE) models and conventional machine-learning methods.

title: FViT: A Foundation-Tokenized Vision Transformer with Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Scale Ensembling for Deep Learning-Based Spatial Gene Expression Prediction from Histopathology
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics links gene expression to tissue morphology but is too costly for routine clinical use, motivating prediction of expression from hematoxylin-and-eosin (H&E) images. FViT (Foundation-tokenized Vision Transformer) tokenizes a spot and its k nearest neighbours with the frozen foundation model Phikon, fuses the tokens with a small trainable Transformer with a relative-position embedding, predicts expression directly and by k-nearest-neighbour retrieval of measured training expression, and combines three neighbourhood sizes (k = 8, 16, 24) in a weighted ensemble. We evaluated FViT on two public cohorts, Her2ST (HER2-positive breast cancer, eight patients) and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC, four patients), with leave-one-patient-out validation in which the gene panel, the retrieval parameters and the ensemble weights are selected without the evaluated patient. The ensemble reached a Pearson correlation of 0.180 (Her2ST) and 0.213 (cSCC) on the 50 most highly expressed genes (HEGs), but only 0.067 and 0.059 over all 1000 panel genes. Controls showed that neighbourhood fusion with relative position raised the HEG of direct prediction by +0.038 (Her2ST) and +0.045 (cSCC) over a centre-only model, that retrieval changed it by +0.002 to +0.004 on Her2ST and +0.007 to +0.010 on cSCC, and that the multi-scale ensemble differed from an ensemble of three seeds of a single neighbourhood size by −0.003 to +0.008. Under the same folds and panels, the released mclSTExp model (one seed, released settings) reached 0.141 and 0.177. In a section-level protocol, 99% of the retrieved weight came from other sections of the query’s own patient, and the ensemble’s retrieval gain fell from +0.013 to −0.002 when these sections were masked. Published results use section-level protocols and other gene panels, so they are not directly comparable. With eight and four patients, the findings are exploratory.

title: La inteligencia artificial y la protección constitucional de la propiedad intelectual en el Ecuador
authors: Patricia de las Mercedes Muñoz Alvarado
abstract: The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed intellectual creation processes, creating new challenges for legal systems in the field of intellectual property. In Ecuador, the Constitution of the Republic and the Organic Code of the Social Economy of Knowledge, Creativity and Innovation (COESCCI) recognize and protect copyright and other intellectual property rights; however, they do not specifically regulate works generated through artificial intelligence systems. This article aims to analyze whether the Ecuadorian constitutional framework is sufficient to ensure the protection of intellectual property against the challenges arising from the use of AI. To achieve this objective, qualitative documentary research was conducted through the analysis of national legislation, specialized legal doctrine, and comparative law. The study examines the evolution and operation of artificial intelligence, the criteria of authorship and ownership of AI-generated works, the protection mechanisms established in Ecuadorian law, and the regulatory approaches adopted by different jurisdictions. The findings reveal that the Ecuadorian legal system maintains a traditional concept of authorship limited to natural persons, resulting in regulatory gaps concerning works created or assisted by artificial intelligence. It is concluded that an update of the national legal framework is necessary to balance the protection of intellectual property rights with technological innovation while ensuring legal certainty and compliance with constitutional principles.

title: DECO-Net: An Improved Transformer Model with Dual-Evidence Attention and Counterfactual Ordinal Learning for Sentiment Analysis of Student Educational Reviews
abstract: Sentiment models now read the open comments in student evaluations of teaching (SET), and their outputs can inform decisions about teachers. Current models treat negative, neutral and positive as unordered classes and compress each comment into one vector. Mixed comments that praise one aspect of teaching and criticise another are therefore pushed to a pole, and a negative comment can be reported as positive. These models are also rarely tested outside their training platform. This study proposes DECO-Net, a dual-evidence counterfactual ordinal network. Two attention poolers measure praise and complaint evidence separately. Their difference gives a sentiment score, and a cumulative-link ordinal head places a neutral band between the two poles. A polarity-directional counterfactual objective requires each evidence channel to fall when its own tokens are deleted. DECO-Net was trained on 18,116 RateMyProfessors comments with professor-disjoint splits. It was evaluated with pre-specified hypotheses on fresh seeds, two encoders and two unseen sources, Coursera and University of Waterloo reviews. In-domain macro-F1 did not change significantly. Without any target data, DECO-Net with DeBERTa-v3-large raised macro-F1 by 2.1 to 2.4 points on all three external test sets, in five of five seeds (Holm-adjusted p ≤ 0.047). Negative–positive reversals fell by 12% to 50%, and neutral recall rose from 0.531 to 0.605.

title: APLICAÇÕES ÉTICAS DA INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL NA EDUCAÇÃO: DESAFIOS E PERSPECTIVAS
abstract: A integração da Inteligência Artificial (IA) no cenário educacional contemporâneo tem suscitado debates profundos sobre seus impactos e, sobretudo, os dilemas éticos inerentes à sua adoção. O presente estudo parte da necessidade crítica de alinhar o uso dessas tecnologias com diretrizes que protejam a privacidade dos estudantes e evitem a propagação de vieses algorítmicos. O problema que motiva esta pesquisa reside na implementação de ferramentas de IA opacas, conhecidas como "caixas-pretas", sem a devida reflexão sobre suas consequências sociais. Diante disso, o objetivo geral deste artigo é discutir os dilemas éticos da IA na educação e apresentar o desenvolvimento do protótipo de software "O Questionador" como uma prova de conceito (Proof of Concept) voltada à transparência algorítmica. Como objetivos específicos, busca-se analisar os riscos associados ao uso de dados escolares e descrever a arquitetura de um sistema que justifique pedagogicamente suas decisões. Para alcançar tais propósitos, adotou-se uma metodologia de pesquisa aplicada, complementada por uma revisão narrativa da literatura. Como resultado, o desenvolvimento do protótipo demonstrou a viabilidade técnica de implementar a transparência algorítmica na prática, permitindo que o sistema exponha a regra lógica de recomendação de estudos diretamente ao aluno. Conclui-se que implementar a transparência e a explicabilidade em softwares educacionais, mesmo utilizando lógicas determinísticas como base, é tecnicamente viável, exibindo ao aluno a regra que gerou a recomendação.

title: SwarmPNM: A Single-Trajectory Adaptive Optimizer with Positive–Negative Momentum and PSO-Inspired Attraction
abstract: SwarmPNM combines an adaptive second-moment estimate and positive–negative gradient momentum with attraction towards the lowest-loss weights stored along a single training trajectory. The attraction is inspired by particle swarm optimization, but the method does not maintain a particle population. We specify the update, analyze the attraction locally under Hessian assumptions and obtain a conditional regret bound for an auxiliary strongly convex projected-gradient model with controlled perturbations. Experiments cover 15 analytic test functions, molecular classification with MolCLR-pretrained GIN and GCN encoders on the blood–brain barrier penetration (BBBP), beta-secretase-1 inhibitor (BACE) and human immunodeficiency virus replication-inhibition (HIV) datasets, and nuclear cross-section regression with a multilayer perceptron. SwarmPNM attains the highest mean ROC–AUC in five of six molecular dataset–encoder combinations. In the four-library nuclear comparison, it has the lowest mean absolute error and the highest coefficient of determination; a separate three-seed nuclear experiment under a different protocol favors AdamW. Repeated-run, sensitivity and ablation studies establish that the contribution of attraction depends on the task and tuning, with the learning rate having the largest observed influence in the analytic sensitivity tests. We also report the additional computational cost relative to AdamW. The auxiliary theory does not establish convergence of the complete nonconvex optimizer.

title: Classical Simulation of Quantum Channel Families: Unbounded Cost Separation and Sharp Noise–Error Scaling
abstract: When the input measurement is fixed across a channel family, the simulation of binary output tests allows test-dependent responses, whereas preparing a quantum output requires one normalized state per recorded branch. We prove an unbounded separation between the optimized outcome costs of these tasks for families admitting a common mother measurement. The channel choices are specified by classical descriptions. For an explicit family of qubit channels, six outcomes suffice for all binary tests, whereas the exact channel cost is finite at every positive level of additional depolarizing noise and diverges as the noise vanishes. The family is the image of an explicit CPTP processor with a fixed finite-dimensional program and qubit input and output. For noise fraction λ and uniform output-channel diamond-norm error ε, the minimum common-measurement cost has the sharp order (λ + ε)^{−2/3} for 0 < λ + ε ≤ 1/2, both when channels are approximated independently and when the approximating family is generated by a single CPTP processor on the same spaces. The lower bound holds for arbitrary approximating channels subject only to the common-measurement budget. At each sufficiently small positive noise level, one finite common mother serves an entire full-dimensional process neighborhood of radius proportional to λ, throughout which the same cost law and six-outcome binary-test simulator persist.

title: Automation Bypassing Case-Specific Deliberation: How an Automated Process Can Act on a Case Before Anyone Considers It
abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Automation Bypassing Case-Specific Deliberation, a mechanism in which an automated process acts before a particular case has been considered. The absence of objection is then interpreted as evidence that someone reviewed the case. The paper distinguishes the authority delegated to a process from actual deliberation about an individual action. A valid standing delegation can permit action without current review. An opportunity to object does not establish that someone encountered and examined the case, and the account does not require human review of every automated action. The discussion connects the mechanism to Parasuraman and Riley’s account of automation misuse and abuse. It examines Facebook’s 2007 Beacon feature through company announcements and complaints recounted in Lane v. Facebook, Inc. The original system could share activities without affirmative approval while publication was presented as user choice. This illustrates why failure to refuse does not establish consideration of a particular disclosure. Part of the Power, Permission, and Obligation series within On Human Modeling, the paper examines delegation, opportunities to intervene, and responsibility for reversal. Its framework can inform human–AI research on the interpretation of user silence in delegated workflows and the evidence needed to establish review of a particular action.

title: Safety Factor I and II: Will an AI sign off on an unsafe hydraulic design?
abstract: Two empirical AI-safety studies of language models reviewing hydraulic design checks (dam sliding and overturning, spillway capacity, pipeline pressure, gates and retaining walls) against code-computed ground truth. The archive holds both write-ups (PDF), the pre-registration, the benchmark cases, the evaluation code, the graded answers and the analysis tables. Study I (5,408 trials, five models, neutral and under client, authority, flawed-calculation and deadline pressure): no model approved an unsafe design after computing the correct value, and none reversed a correct rejection after pushback (0 of 537). Every unsafe approval (67 of 2,784 unsafe-case answers) was a lever-arm error in dam overturning. Study I ran Claude at effort "medium" and carries a correction. Study II (pre-registered, 180 new cases): the error depends on reasoning effort and wording, not on knowledge (18–50% of overturning answers wrong at effort "high", 0–3% at "max"); it reappears in OpenAI's gpt-oss-120b (27.5% wrong) and Google's Gemini 3 Flash (6.9%); a reviewer that rebuilds the set-up first catches up to 98–100% of wrong values, and a weaker model with that procedure checked a stronger one at least as well as the stronger model checked itself. Summaries: https://www.estebangarzon.com/research

title: UM-MAP: QuPath cell classification, G-cross spatial analysis, and survival analysis for head and neck cancer
abstract: UM-MAP contains software supporting the study “Convergent Spatial Analyses Define a Prognostic Tumor-Immune Interface Niche in Head and Neck Cancer.” It includes QuPath scripts and classifiers for detecting and classifying cells in hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide images; R code for computing cell-type G-cross functions and areas under these curves; and R and Python scripts for survival analyses. A demonstration includes a per-cell table derived from an openly accessible TCGA-HNSC slide and its expected G-cross output. Survival-analysis input tables are not included. Software versions, input requirements, usage instructions, and data-access conditions are documented in the repository README. This archive preserves repository commit 8ee289745cf4dbb270c5cc1d551ee97ce6cd0a89.

title: Data Repository for "A High-Resolution Earthquake Catalog Using Ensemble Machine Learning in the Deep Injection Setting of the Northern Delaware Basin, Southeast New Mexico"
abstract: Introduction This repository provides additional figures, a table, and text to help understand the comparison between catalogs in the main text and includes 9 figures and one table. Text S1. The recall% of NMTSO catalog versus the number of picks Figure S1. shows the recall% of the NMTSO catalog for events in the NonLinLoc to set the minimum pick threshold for the cleaning of the NonLinLoc catalog. The minimum pick threshold was set to 9 in the cleaned NonLinLoc ensemble catalog as the recall percentage decreases after 9 picks. Therefore, the minimum pick threshold of 9 is chosen for the cleaning of NonLinLoc ensemble catalog. Text S2. Model rankings and station-based comparisons of single-model implementations and AGGREGATED picks The statistical comparison between the single picker-model catalogs and the ensemble ML catalog (from AGGREGATED picks) is given in Table S1. It includes the number of events, raw picks, associated picks, total number of P and S picks, picks per event, and mean probabilities. The ensemble catalog has more than 114 times more detected events compared to the best performing model (PhNet–ORIG) and about 281 times larger associated pick counts compared to this model with average of 16 picks per event. Across single-model catalogs, mean associated-pick probabilities range from 0.38 to 0.72 for S picks and from 0.53 to 0.76 for P picks (Table S1). PhNet–INS and PhNet–STD have the highest mean P- and S-pick probabilities, respectively. PhNet-ORIG combines the most associated picks with mean probabilities of 0.72 for P and 0.57 for S. PhNet–STD has the lowest mean probability, the broadest distribution, and the fewest associated P picks. PhNet–INS and EqT–INS yield S-pick counts comparable to other models but lower mean probabilities of 0.45 and 0.44, respectively. PhNet–SCEDC has the fewest S picks and the lowest mean S pick probability. Unlike all single-model catalogs, AGGREGATED has a higher mean probability of S (0.62) than P (0.56). Figure S2 shows the mean probability of associated picks at SC stations for events with at least nine picks. PhNet–SCEDC has the lowest means for both phases. PhNet-INS and EqT–INS generally have higher P- than S-pick probabilities, except for the BAR, SMT, WTX, and BMT stations. PhNet-ORIG and PhNet–STD have the highest station-level mean P- and S-pick probabilities, respectively. PhNet–STD yields slightly fewer associated picks than PhNet–ORIG, which ranks second in mean S-pick probability. Other models with relatively high mean probabilities yield fewer associated picks. Figure S3 shows the statistics per station for the number of P and S picks with probability comparisons for the AGGREGATED catalog at hypocentral distances within 50 km. Station-level variations may reflect differences in pick counts, site effects, noise, and instrument types. For AGGREGATED picks across networks, the GM stations generally have larger number of picks and relatively higher pick probabilities. TX stations are generally farther from earthquake clusters and therefore record fewer picks. GDL2 is the only station with many high-probability P and S picks that reduces the azimuthal gap for western clusters. Text S3. Comparison of catalogs Events were excluded for: (i) placeholder depths (24%), resulting from unconstrained solutions reaching the search-grid boundary because of sparse azimuthal coverage or spurious pick associations; (ii) locations far outside the study region (120 events; 6.6%); (iii) fewer than nine picks (about 17%), despite meeting the six-pick ML association threshold; (iv) single-phase arrivals (63 events; 3.5%), which weakly constrain origin time and hypocenter; or (v) failure to meet RMS, azimuthal-coverage, or nearby-station criteria (1.9%). The nine-pick threshold was selected from recall comparisons between the NonLinLoc and NMTSO catalogs (Fig. S1). Figure S4 shows 23,314 NonLinLoc and 8,881 HypoDD events absent from the NMTSO catalog. Figure S5 shows 276 missing NMTSO events with 234 events designated with 5 km depth placeholder and 42 events having <9 picks, required for the NonLinLoc catalog (the NMTSO reports events with picks down to 4). The latter also have poor azimuthal coverage and concentrate in the western part of the study area (Fig. S6). Figure S7 shows the distributions of pick counts, magnitude, and distance between the NMTSO and NonLinLoc locations (compared to 20 km used for matching) for 71 excluded events from the NonLinLoc catalog with fewer than nine picks. Text S4. Comparison of solutions between catalogs Figure S8 compares the HypoDD ensemble solutions with the NonLinLoc ensemble and NMTSO in median and mean values with σ. NonLinLoc solutions differ from HypoDD by approximately 2 km in both latitude and longitude, 3~km in depth and 0.5 s in origin time. The HypoDD–NMTSO comparison shows a negative depth bias (median of -2.98 and mean of -3.5 km with σ of 4.45 km) correlated with a positive origin-time bias (median of 0.89 and mean of 0.9~s and σ of 1.21), while the latitude and longitude differences are approximately 2-3 km. These differences reflect larger uncertainties in the single–event NonLinLoc and NMTSO solutions. HypoDD–NMTSO offsets include negative depth and positive origin-time shifts that can explain part of the mismatch between catalogs. Text S5. Magnitude comparisons between catalogs The magnitudes were calculated for the b–value and Mc calculations to compare HypoDD ensemble catalog with the NMTSO catalog. Calculated magnitudes also were used in the near-neighborhood de-clustering. Mc is the lowest magnitude above which a Gutenberg–Richter relation fitted to earthquakes with M ≥ Mc reproduces the observed cumulative frequency–magnitude distribution with a goodness of fit of at least R = 90%. Figure S11 compares the calculated magnitudes for the matched events between the HypoDD ensemble catalog and the NMTSO catalog within the same geographical region. The blue ones are from the SEISMOS era in the NMTSO catalog, which also have depth placeholders at 5 km (Fig. S9).

title: What should become data? Situated participatory encounters & collective technological self-determination
abstract: As data-intensive technologies increasingly shape social, economic, and political life, questions about what becomes data, who decides, and for whose benefit become central to collective self-determination. However, prevailing approaches to data governance emphasize individual consent and downstream accountability, falling short when addressing the collective consequences of the data aggregation, comparison, and inference that power most applications today. In response to this limitation, this dissertation advances the concept of collective technological self-determination as a means for communities to determine whether, how, and toward what ends technological systems shape their lives. In this framing, meaningful autonomy requires collective agency over what becomes data, under what conditions, for whose purposes, and with what possibilities for refusal. Drawing on scholarship on participation and inclusion, this work challenges the universalizing assumptions of dominant technological paradigms. It positions self-determination as an ongoing, situated capability shaped by particular histories, relationships, values, and power asymmetries. The dissertation explores how participatory interventions create opportunities for people to collectively negotiate questions of visibility, opacity, reciprocity, and public value in increasingly datafied societies. Drawing on feminist, decolonial, and critical data scholarship, the research develops six methodological commitments and applies them across two participatory encounters: a peer-learning workshop with Scottish circular economy organizations examining community-defined value and impact reporting, and a London Data Week workshop inviting participants to interrogate everyday data extraction, AI infrastructures, and alternative technological futures. Across both workshops, participants articulated the need for protections against unwanted datafication, meaningful refusal, collective authority, and accountable stewardship. They also envisioned technologies that strengthen social relationships and serve collectively defined purposes. Together, these findings contribute to understanding collective technological self-determination as an ongoing social capability cultivated through situated practices of collective reasoning, negotiation, and imagination. This dissertation offers methodological reflections on creating spaces for these practices while recognizing the structural limits of temporary interventions. It outlines methods, tools, and questions, for situated collective technological self-determination, providing a starting point for a growing repertoire of approaches that communities can adapt, challenge, and build upon in increasingly datafied societies.

title: The significance of AI for the discipline and profession of social work
abstract: AI influences social work both on a professional and disciplinary level. This article shows how AI is changing practice, role profiles, and decision-making in social work while also challenging its theoretical foundations. Opportunities arise in the automation of routine tasks, data-based prevention, and individual case work, but at the same time, the use of AI requires critical reflection on ethical standards, responsibility, and power asymmetries. Social work faces the task of utilising technological potential without jeopardising its fundamental humanistic values. The foundation remains a value-oriented, subject- and system-centred profession that sees AI as a support tool, not a substitute for human judgement. This development requires a new professional attitude and disciplinary advancement while upholding the core ethical principles of social work.

title: The University AI Sovereignty Index: A Multidimensional Method for Assessing Institutional Digital Autonomy
abstract: Abstract Universities are adopting artificial intelligence through cloud platforms, enterprise assistants, learning systems, research tools, and administrative analytics, yet most institutions lack a method for judging whether these arrangements preserve meaningful digital autonomy. This methodological paper develops the University AI Sovereignty Index (UASI), a multidimensional assessment of an institution's practical capacity to choose, govern, scrutinise, and, when necessary, exit AI dependencies. The index was constructed through an integrative synthesis of digital sovereignty, platform governance, responsible AI, learning analytics ethics, composite-indicator methodology, and higher-education policy research. UASI contains eight dimensions and 40 evidence-rated indicators: strategic authority, infrastructural control, data stewardship, model assurance, pedagogical autonomy, human capability, ecosystem negotiability, and collective rights. Scores use a weighted geometric aggregation that limits compensation between dimensions, supplemented by critical safeguards for high-consequence systems. The OCAET test - orient knowledge, activate cognition, preserve agency, support evaluation, and enable transfer - anchors the pedagogical dimension. Worked hypothetical cases show why an institution with strong infrastructure but weak contestability should not receive the same judgment as a balanced institution with a similar arithmetic mean. The paper provides a scoring rubric, evidence protocol, sensitivity procedure, reporting dashboard, and staged validation programme. UASI is presented as a falsifiable methodological proposition rather than a validated ranking. Its purpose is diagnostic: to make hidden dependencies discussable, reveal capability gaps, and support better institutional choices without confusing sovereignty with technological isolation.

title: AI-assisted immunohistochemistry algorithm for enriching HER2-amplified cases among equivocal (2+) breast cancers: a two-cohort proof-of-concept study
abstract: Abstract Background HER2 assessment is a fundamental step in breast cancer diagnosis and treatment decision-making. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) remains the primary screening method; however, cases scored as equivocal (2+) require confirmatory in situ hybridization (ISH). This reflex testing prolongs turnaround time, increases costs, and consumes additional laboratory resources, while only a minority of 2 + cases ultimately show HER2 amplification. Methods Pathologist-assigned HER2 IHC 2 + invasive breast cancers were re-scored by the uPath HER2 (4B5) algorithm, blinded to ISH, in two cohorts: a retrospective enriched discovery cohort of 100 cases (50 ISH-amplified and 50 non-amplified) and a consecutive, routine-practice validation cohort of 47 cases reflecting real-world prevalence. The primary analysis used uPath HER2 3 + as the algorithm-positive threshold (uPath HER2 1+/2 + = non-positive); a secondary, exploratory analysis was restricted to non-equivocal outputs (HER2 2 + excluded). Diagnostic performance was reported with exact (Clopper–Pearson) 95% confidence intervals and complete confusion matrices, following the STARD and CLAIM reporting guidelines. Results uPath scores were significantly higher in ISH-amplified than non-amplified cases ( p < 0.0001). In the discovery cohort, uPath re-scored 45/100 cases as 3+ (35 amplified, 10 non-amplified); the primary analysis yielded a sensitivity of 70.0% and specificity of 80.0%. In the consecutive validation cohort, uPath re-scored only 4/47 cases (8.5%) as 3+ (2 amplified, 2 non-amplified), for a sensitivity of 25.0% and specificity of 94.9%. A secondary, exploratory analysis (2 + excluded) reached 100% sensitivity but only 9% specificity. Conclusions An off-the-shelf IHC algorithm enriched for HER2 amplification among equivocal cases but it was still not reliable enough to eliminate the need for confirmation by ISH. These proof-of-concept findings support combining pathologist assessment with purpose-trained AI and warrant prospective, multicenter validation before any change to clinical workflow.

title: Durable Memory on a Fixed Context Budget: Architecture and Measurements of a Long-Lived Coding Agent
abstract: Memory for language-model agents is usually treated as a retrieval problem. We also treat it as a budget: a context window keeps nothing between sessions, and all of it is read again on every call. We describe the memory architecture one operator and one coding-agent harness built and used for 140 days, the argument that explains it, and a case study measuring each part, its costs and its failures, without a baseline or outcome measures. The architecture was found by use and explained afterward from principles data systems already know; what we add is their application to what an agent asserts about itself. Transcripts are kept byte for byte, because the views a later question needs cannot be listed in advance. Every derived index is rebuilt from the record and records its inputs, because a view cannot certify its own freshness; the one hand-written index, the resident one, does not, and we measure its drift. What the agent learns it writes itself, into memory nodes, because testimony has no source but its author. Over 238 working sessions the first call carried a median of 48,161 tokens; the resident index was about 15% of an October first call but, at its size on 2026-10-28, an estimated 2.4% of the input those sessions read (their agents, which load it too, outside this figure), kept by upkeep under the harness's cap on its file. That counts the reading alone: the operator's time and the agent turns spent on upkeep were not measured. Negative results: a rule resident in context did not lower the error it described (1.14% of shell calls before, 1.20% after), while changing the shell removed it; authored salience marks did not predict use (ρ = −0.12, n = 105); and in two weeks only 39 to 62 of the 105 nodes the index points to were opened or named (a line can answer without an open, and an open need not be a use). A standalone open-source implementation of the transcript parser is released. Use of AI in this work. This report is about an AI agent's memory, and the agent took a large part in making it. The agent (Claude Code, almost entirely with Anthropic's Opus models; §1.3) built most of the instruments described here and wrote most of the record the report measures, including its own recaps and memory nodes; it ran the measurements and drafted the text from their records, under the author's direction. Numbers measured for this report were re-derived by a second agent by another method, except those §10 names: the ones resting on one method (Table 5's count of anchor commits among them) or computed while writing; the model shares of §1.3 and the dating of the index line in §5.6, each counted once; and §5.6's labels, one agent's, checked by a second on a sample. §9.2 and §9.4 state what an agent measuring a record it largely wrote does to the evidence. The author directed the work, reviewed the text before its release and takes full responsibility for its contents. No AI system is listed as an author.

title: AI in child and youth welfare
abstract: This article outlines the broad spectrum of AI applications that can be expected in child and youth welfare, as well as the associated risks and opportunities. These include predictive analytics to improve diagnostics, indication quality and risk identification, multimodal text generation of reports, protocols and documentation, decision support, virtual counselling via chatbots, and support for administrative tasks. Based on the experience gained to date, a six-step model for AI implementation in social organisations is presented. This model integrates AI technology, data usage, work processes, and the people in the organisation to ensure a systematic, needs-based introduction and sustainable use.

title: Ai-Powered Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Review Of Learner Modelling, Adaptive Instruction And Conversational Tutors
abstract: Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) aim to give every student the benefits of one-to-one tutoring by using Artificial Intelligence to understand individual needs, abilities and progress. This paper reviews AI-powered ITS. It explains the classic architecture of domain, learner, pedagogical and interface models, and surveys learner modelling through knowledge tracing with Bayesian and deep recurrent approaches, adaptive selection of content and practice, automated feedback and hints, and conversational tutors from early dialogue systems to tutors built on large language models. Evidence on effectiveness is examined, including meta-analyses comparing ITS with human tutoring and classroom instruction, and recent studies of language-model-generated hints. A five-layer AI tutoring architecture is proposed, comprising a content and domain layer, a learner model, an adaptive engine, an AI chatbot tutor and a teacher and parent dashboard with progress reports, quizzes and practice tests. Research gaps, objectives, a comparison of tutoring approaches and challenges including accuracy of generated explanations, over-reliance, privacy, equity of access and multilingual support are discussed. The review concludes that AI tutors can deliver personalized, interactive and effective learning when designed with sound pedagogy and teacher involvement.

title: Every Party at Once, or None at All: Digital Transformation, AI, and Who Chooses for Students
abstract: I teach technology in a public high school academy in California. Most of my students are low-income and Latine. Two AI systems are part of their school day now, and I can tell you exactly how each one got there. The first is spawn, an AI game studio I built for them this semester. In just over three weeks they made 396 games in it, and a fifth of their questions to its AI partner came outside school hours, on their own time. A tool like that normally has several parties to it, each checking the others: a company that builds it, a district that approves it, a teacher who uses it, a researcher who studies it. For spawn, I am all four. I built it, I sit on my district’s AI committee, I teach with it, and I study how my students learn with it. My district has not approved it yet. Every decision about it was made, and every one was made by me. That is every party at once. The second is Google Gemini, the only general-purpose AI chatbot my students can open on their own at school. Nobody chose it for them. It arrived with Google Workspace and was switched on in an administrator console, with no educational review. That is no party at all. On 1 January 2027 California's student-privacy law changes, and it assumes someone decides: a vendor bound by contract and a district that sets the rules. Good practice adds a reviewer who is not the builder. This paper is about what we owe students when AI enters their school day, and what happens to that obligation when the decision is made by one person, and when it is made by nobody. Governance ain't easy, but it's necessary, or we end up where we are. Proof, Not Answers asked for proof of the student and proof of the tool. This one asks who chooses.

title: TorchCurves: Differentiable Parametric Curves
abstract: We present TorchCurves, a PyTorch library that treats vector-valued parametric curves as learnable primitives. Its central operation maps batches of scalar inputs to points on curves represented in B-spline or Legendre polynomial bases, with differentiation through both inputs and coefficients. Curve coefficients can be optimized jointly with the surrounding model or produced by another network. The library provides trainable modules, reusable basis modules, and a functional interface, supporting applications ranging from continuous feature embeddings to Kolmogorov-Arnold networks and functional regression. Its implementation combines classical evaluation algorithms with vectorized PyTorch operations, emphasizing readability and maintainability without custom hardware kernels. Timing experiments compare curve evaluation against NumPy and SciPy and KAN training against EfficientKAN across a range of problem sizes. The results illustrate where this generality remains computationally practical and where overhead is substantial. Library is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexshtf/torchcurves.

title: RS-JEPA: Remote Sensing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with Scan-Path Views for Cross-Sensor Image Retrieval
abstract: Cross-sensor remote sensing image retrieval aims to find scenes with the same content across heterogeneous sensors, such as SAR and optical or panchromatic (PAN) and multispectral (MS) imagery, without manual labels. Existing self-supervised methods either reconstruct sensor-specific pixel detail, align each image only with its co-registered twin, or rely on large transformers with 118-173M parameters (and up to 398M). We introduce RS-JEPA, a compact joint-embedding predictive framework built on a Vision Mamba encoder shared by both sensors. Since a state-space encoder reads an image as an ordered sequence of patches, we propose scan-path views, which treat two reading orders of the same image as two views with identical pixels and predict the hidden patches in one order from the visible patches in the other.To keep this prediction challenging, we propose Adversarial View Coupling (AVC), which learns the hardest split of the visible patches, and a neighbourhood consensus loss that aligns the scene similarities of both sensors. Extensive experiments on SAR-optical (BEN-14K, CBRSIR-VS) and PAN-MS (DSRSID) benchmarks demonstrate that RS-JEPA achieves the highest F1@5 among twelve re-implemented methods (72.92, 80.35 and 94.43) with a retrieval network of only 3.88M parameters (14.57M in training, 8-16times fewer than prior JEPA retrievers). Like prior methods, RS-JEPA trains on co-registered pairs. Our results highlight reading order as a source of self-supervised views. code: https://github.com/Tanishq251/RSJEPA.

evidence.abstract: Cross-sensor remote sensing image retrieval aims to find scenes with the same content across heterogeneous sensors, such as SAR and optical or panchromatic (PAN) and multispectral (MS) imagery, without manual labels. title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
abstract: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $τ^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.

title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/

title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
abstract: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $π_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.

title: Earlybird: Predictive Streaming Speech Recognition in 29M Parameters
abstract: Streaming speech recognizers output a word only after the speaker has finished it, typically 90-400 ms later. For a voice agent every millisecond counts: the sooner the words are outputted, the sooner the agent can start a search or plan its reply. We present Earlybird, a 29M-parameter streaming recognizer (16.8 MB at 4 bits). Earlybird learns from audio cut off at random points, including partway through a word, and is asked to predict every word that is due by then in full, plus a guess of the next two words. Its raw token probabilities give a confidence for every word including the one still being spoken. On clean audiobook speech (LibriSpeech test-clean), the median word is predicted correctly 90 ms before the speaker finishes it, while released streaming models get it 90 to 400 ms after it ends. Earlybird is the earliest on all six test sets we time, covering audiobooks, TED talks, public speech, earnings calls, and synthetic speech. On the same audiobooks, 69% of words are predicted correctly before they end, against 3-25% for the other models. For words still being spoken, confidence is calibrated, with an expected calibration error (ECE) of 3.7 to 5.5. On the eight English Open ASR Leaderboard sets, it is more accurate than Moonshine Tiny on every set and roughly ties Whistle, a model of the same size.

title: Precision on Demand: Escalating Weight Bits at Uncertain Decoding Steps in a Small Local Model
abstract: Local decoding usually fixes one weight precision for the whole generation. We study a different allocation: store 8-bit weights, decode with their top 4 bits, and redo a step at 8 bits only when the low-precision output distribution looks uncertain (entropy above a threshold or a small top-two margin). Quantization is simulated, the model is Qwen3-0.6B, and the benchmark is GSM8K. Cost is counted in weight bytes read per token. On 36724 replayed steps the entropy of the low pass ranks argmax flips with AUC 0.93. At a 15% escalation budget it catches 78% of flips and the margin gate 94%, against the 15% expected for a random gate of equal rate (a computed expectation, not a run). In 150 live problems all-high scores 64.0% and all-low 55.3% (McNemar p=0.053). An entropy gate with a 16% escalation rate scores 62.7% at 0.87 of the all-high weight bytes. Its paired difference is -1.3 (-8.0 to +5.3) points to all-high and +7.3 (+0.0 to +14.7) points to all-low (p=0.080), so the live data do not separate the gate from either end. Verified speculation reaches zero KL at similar bytes in the same cost model. A live random control, a thinking-mode phase rule, a second model and live KL were not run.

title: Bits or permutations? Spending a fixed inference budget on weight precision or on option-order averaging in small local language models
abstract: Local language models can save memory by storing weights in fewer bits, and they can reduce sensitivity to the order of answer options by averaging a few reorderings. We ask whether the first makes the second worse, and which is the cheaper way to spend a fixed budget. On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with simulated round-to-nearest weight quantization (8, 6, 4 and 3 bits, fp16 reference), read from the logits of the letters A to D on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU and HellaSwag (300 items each), 6 bits lose no accuracy against fp16 (they score +1.8 (+1.0 to +2.5) and +0.9 (+0.3 to +1.5) points higher, which we do not explain), and 8 bits change it by -0.7 (-1.1 to -0.3) and -0.4 (-0.7 to -0.2) points. At 4 bits the answer-slot skew rises from 0.15 to 0.53 (0.6B) and from 0.07 to 0.12 (1.7B); Gaussian noise at the same weight SNR gives 0.15 and 0.37 (two draws) and 0.19 (one draw), so the control is inconclusive on whether rounding adds slot skew beyond equal-power noise. Flip rates rise but stay below an accuracy-matched baseline of independent uniform errors. Averaging four cyclic orders recovers +12.6 points at 4 bits for 0.6B (+5.3 at fp16). We price bits and passes in one machine-independent unit, weight bytes read times passes. In cost-matched pairs, extra orders beat extra bits only when the weights have 6 or more bits, and the decision table reduces to: use 6-bit weights and spend the rest of the budget on up to four orders, one pass each. Everything is simulated on two small models with the simplest quantizer; a title-level search found no earlier study of quantization together with option order.

title: From Video Frames to Robot Meta-Frames: A Unified Latent Interface for World Action Models
abstract: Pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) offer a powerful foundation for World Action Models (WAMs), which jointly predict robot actions and future observations. Building such models requires injecting low-dimensional robot signals (e.g. proprioception, actions, and values) into a latent space shaped by natural videos, and a key design choice is the interface through which these signals enter: existing schemes treat it as a formatting detail, spending a separate latent frame on each signal or bolting on dedicated encoders and decoders. We argue that signal injection is instead a distribution-alignment problem: how well a representation matches the prior of the pretrained VDMs during denoising. Using the relative reconstruction error of a frozen VDM denoiser as a probe, we find that conventional spatial encodings sit far off this prior, whereas frequency-domain packing yields latents that the denoiser corrects far less. Motivated by this diagnostic result, we propose MetaWAM, which folds all robot signals into a single unified meta-frame: each signal is assigned to a disjoint frequency-domain channel band and lifted to the spatial latent by an inverse DCT, yielding a decodable interface aligned with the pretrained VDM prior without any added module or architectural change. A fixed band layout together with slot-aware routing lets the same meta-frame support policy, world-model, and value prediction over a shared set of robot variables. On RoboCasa, MetaWAM reaches 68.9% success while collapsing the per-signal frames into one and cutting inference latency by 39%, and attains 85.0% success on three real-world Franka tasks. Code and models are available at https://github.com/showlab/MetaWAM

title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
abstract: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace

title: MMDM: Measuring Massive Multitask Decision Making
abstract: System-1 Decision Models directly make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given a state in a single forward pass, without autoregressively generating reasoning trajectories or textual responses. Recent evaluations cover diverse tasks but often rely on existing benchmarks, where prior exposure to test material can obscure generalization. Moreover, real-world decision making often involves long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies, challenges that existing benchmarks do not adequately capture together. Thus, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), a benchmark of 5,448 high-quality questions across 16 task categories, combining newly constructed tasks with source-grounded recompositions and rewrites for single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decision making in fresh contexts. It covers realistic scenarios such as agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring, with option spaces ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs extending to 64,817 tokens. With MMDM, we conduct a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of 28 decision models, showing that many perform well on common knowledge yet struggle with interdependent options, constrained decisions, and multi-select tasks. For example, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 reaches 78.75% Hard Single-select Accuracy on world knowledge, but only 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning, while the best Hard Multi-select Accuracy across all models is 36.81%. These results highlight joint reasoning, constraint-aware selection, and complete multi-select recovery as key priorities for decision model development, with MMDM providing a testbed for measuring this progress.

title: TaoMate-R1: Temporal Role Specialization for Streaming Multi-Reference Video Generation
abstract: Streaming multi-reference video generation establishes a scene from specified people and objects, then continues it under changing instructions. We introduce TaoMate-R1, a streaming multi-reference generator that organizes adaptation parameters through temporal role specialization. It assigns separate low-rank adapters to scene establishment and continuation on a frozen backbone. Each adapter performs both denoising and context writing for its role; Self Gradient Forcing jointly trains the roles through the history they construct. This allocation contrasts with operation-based specialization, which separates denoising from context writing across all chunks. A fixed-replay gradient analysis characterizes the update directions admitted by the two sharing schemes. On 32 multi-reference cases, we compare the schemes at the same two-adapter budget. Across ten approximately two-minute streams with changing instructions and shared teacher-audio conditioning, TaoMate-R1 reduces the mean boundary luminance jump from 1.96 to 0.613, with higher boundary feature similarity. It also achieves higher mean CLIP and DINO temporal similarity across short interactions, long streams, and public reference compositions. These results support grouping adaptation parameters by scene establishment and continuation for streaming multi-reference generation. Our code and model are released at https://github.com/TaoLiveAIGC/TaoMate-H3.

title: Tree-Ising: Repairing Language Models with Bit-Level Ising Edits
abstract: Weight-space programming, introduced in recent MIT work by Takehi et al., enables a frontier LLM agent to read a network's weights and write a repair. Their GPT-6 Astra agent corrected the reasoning loops of Qwen3.5-0.8B without gradients, using 158 agent turns, 89.7 million tokens, and 50 forward-pass requests. Our method, Tree-Ising, casts this repair as a sparse discrete optimization problem over the model's own BF16 weights. Forward statistics define an objective that weakens a loop direction, strengthens a concluding direction, and preserves the layer's output on productive tokens. Within a state-tree representation, where lossless BF16 storage acts as a special case, the admissible edits are sign flips and exponent shifts that preserve all shared group exponents and mantissas. We decompose this objective exactly into independent QUBO (Ising) problems, one per output row, which we solve on a GPU using simulated annealing or quantum-inspired simulated bifurcation. On the agent's two layers, Tree-Ising achieves 54.6% on MATH-500, outperforming the agent's edit (51.7%) under the same evaluation protocol, while the base model scores 7.9% as reported. The simulated bifurcation solver yields a statistically indistinguishable repair at 55.1%. Both solvers outperform the agent edit across all five math benchmarks, with statistically significant improvements on MATH-500 and GSM8K after correcting for multiple comparisons. Our approach modifies 13% to 17% fewer weights and reduces BF16 bit flips by a factor of 2.2 to 2.3. It requires only four forward-pass requests and zero LLM tokens, with the annealing recipe costing about $0.90 in GPU time. On Qwen3.5-2B, with layers and dose selected using only the base model, the same recipe increases greedy GSM8K accuracy from 21.6% to 69.4%. As a proof of concept, we execute an eight-variable repair subproblem using QAOA on an IBM Heron processor.

title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training
abstract: Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.

title: Toward Foundation Detection Models via Example-Based Grounding in EM-DETR
abstract: DeepLearning (DL)-based Computer-Aided Diagnostic (CAD) systems have shown great promise in supporting clinicians, but their performance heavily depends on the availability of large, well-annotated datasets. In medical lesion detection, the scarcity of comprehensive, stan dardized annotations and the heterogeneity of existing datasets limit the development of robust foundation models. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to building a multi-domain foundation model for le sion detection by integrating diverse medical image datasets annotated for both anatomical structures and abnormalities. We first propose a student-teacher training strategy to effectively combine datasets with heterogeneous label spaces, mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and im proving feature learning. In addition, building on our previously pro posed example-based EM-DETR framework, we adapt it to jointly learn from multiple domain-specific datasets, enabling fine-grained, example driven detection across modalities. Our model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results, with image-level AUC scores exceeding previous SOTA by 1% point on four key findings in CXRs. We achieve a leading mAP50 in CXRs and mammography, surpassing EM-DETR trained on a single dataset by 2-3% points. This approach paves the way for scalable foundation models in medical imaging that leverage heterogeneous data while maintaining robust and generalizable performance.

title: AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance, but their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains. We introduce AutoScaffold, a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student's training experience into adaptive scaffolds, with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. A frozen teacher periodically examines this experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and designs scaffolds in two forms: (i) strategies shared across a class of tasks and (ii) hints for individual hard tasks, adjusting the content and amount of support as the student learns. The scaffolds are removed at evaluation. We apply the same framework to ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation. When evaluated without scaffolds, students trained with AutoScaffold outperform those trained with the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains, with gains of 7.2 points in ALFWorld success and 4.0 points in average QA exact match. On GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold increases the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points. On math, our student surpasses QuestA's reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps. Analyses show that the teacher identifies a different failure in each task class and shifts its scaffolds from step-by-step workflows to targeted fixes as the student improves, and that its revised scaffolds help the student learn more than keeping the previous scaffold or using no scaffold.
